lede: Log lines, event tags and product attributes rarely share one fixed set of fields: a checkout line carries an order reference, a device line a firmware version. A map column holds whatever keys each row has, and you read, list and reshape them by key.
objectives: Read a value from a map by key, and predict what a missing key gives
List a map's keys and values, count them and check for a key
Turn a map into key and value rows with `F.explode`
Build and combine maps, and parse JSON text with changing keys into a map

blocks.md:
`application_logs` has one row per structured log line from several services: when it was logged, its `level`, the `service`, a `message`, and `attributes`, a **map** from text keys to text values. `application_logs_raw` is the same log file before parsing: one line of text per row, in a column called `value`. Both are loaded as DataFrames, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

A struct has the same fields on every row, fixed by the schema. A map doesn't: each row has its own keys. Every line here has `host`, but only checkout lines have `order_ref`, and only gateway lines have `device_id`.

blocks.title: A column of maps
blocks.note: `attributes` is a `map` with `string` keys and `string` values. `show` prints each map as `{key -> value, ...}`, and the keys differ from service to service.

blocks.md:
Read a value by its key with brackets, `F.col("attributes")["region"]`, or with `.getItem("region")`. A dot path, `"attributes.region"`, works on maps too.

A row that doesn't have the key gives NULL, with no error. All values in this map are text, even numbers like `latency_ms`.

blocks.title: Look up keys
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

application_logs.select(
    "log_id", "service",
    F.col("attributes")["region"].alias("region"),
    F.col("attributes").getItem("device_id").alias("device_id"),
    F.col("attributes.latency_ms").alias("latency_ms"),
).show()
blocks.note: Only the gateway lines have a `device_id`; everywhere else it's NULL. The two lines from background jobs have no `region` and no `latency_ms`.

blocks.md:
To look at the keys themselves:

- `F.map_keys(col)` and `F.map_values(col)` give arrays of the keys and of the values.
- `F.size(col)` counts the entries, as it does for arrays.
- `F.map_contains_key(col, key)` is true when the row has that key.

blocks.title: Keys, values and counts
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

application_logs.select(
    "log_id",
    F.map_keys("attributes").alias("keys"),
    F.size("attributes").alias("entries"),
    F.map_contains_key("attributes", "order_ref").alias("has_order_ref"),
).show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: Two checkout lines carry an `order_ref`. The keys come back in the order they were stored.

blocks.md: `F.explode` on a map gives **one row per entry**, with two columns, the key and the value. Name them with `.alias("key", "value")`. A row with an empty map gives no rows. This long shape is handy when you don't know the keys in advance.

blocks.title: One row per key
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

entries = application_logs.select("log_id", F.explode("attributes").alias("key", "value"))
entries.show(12)
print(entries.count(), "entries from", application_logs.count(), "log lines")
blocks.note: Each line becomes as many rows as it has keys: 43 entries from 10 lines.

blocks.md: You can build maps as well. `F.create_map(key1, value1, key2, value2, ...)` takes keys and values in pairs; `F.lit("level")` makes a column holding the same text on every row, to use as a key. `F.map_concat(m1, m2)` joins two maps into one. The maps must not share a key: by default a repeated key stops the job.

blocks.title: Build and combine maps
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

extra = F.create_map(F.lit("service"), F.col("service"), F.lit("level"), F.col("level"))

application_logs.select("log_id", F.map_concat("attributes", extra).alias("all_attributes")).show(3, truncate=False)
blocks.note: Each map gains two entries at the end. None of the lines already had a `service` or `level` key, so nothing clashes.

blocks.md: Maps are also how you parse JSON whose keys change from row to row. In `F.from_json`, give the changing part a map type, `MAP<STRING, STRING>`, instead of a struct with fixed fields. Lines that aren't valid JSON give missing values, as before; here three lines of the raw log are broken.

blocks.title: Parse changing keys into a map
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

parsed = application_logs_raw.select(F.from_json("value", "log_id STRING, attributes MAP<STRING, STRING>").alias("log"))
parsed.printSchema()
parsed.select("log.log_id", F.size("log.attributes").alias("entries"), F.col("log.attributes")["host"].alias("host")).show()
blocks.note: Every good line keeps all its keys, whatever they are. So `entries` changes from line to line. The three broken lines give NULL in every column: a map type makes changing keys readable, not broken JSON.

concept.prompt: A row's `attributes` map has no `device_id` key. What does `F.col("attributes")["device_id"]` give?
concept.why: Looking up a key the map doesn't have gives NULL.

concept.prompt: Why use a map instead of a struct for `attributes`?
choices: The keys differ from row to row, and a struct's fields are fixed by the schema
concept.why: A struct has the same fields on every row. A map holds whatever keys each row brings.

concept.prompt: A log line's map has 4 entries. How many rows does `F.explode("attributes")` give for it?
concept.why: One row per entry, each with its key and value: 4 rows.

review: A map holds keys and values that differ from row to row; a struct's fields are fixed.
Read a value with `F.col("m")["key"]`, `.getItem("key")` or `"m.key"`; a missing key gives NULL.
`F.map_keys`, `F.map_values`, `F.size` and `F.map_contains_key` describe a map without opening it up.
`F.explode` on a map gives one row per entry; name the columns with `.alias("key", "value")`.
`F.create_map` builds a map from key and value pairs; `F.map_concat` combines maps that don't share keys.
Parse JSON with changing keys using a `MAP<STRING, STRING>` type in `F.from_json`.
